newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Music on Internet needs copyright defence.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Music on Internet needs copyright defence.

text.p: The global music industry could lose millions of dollars in revenues unless countries urgently implement copyright laws to protect artists whose recordings are played on the Internet, officials said on Thursday.
The on-line delivery of music is now in its infancy but, according to some forecasts, may grow into a market worth billions of dollars during the next decade.
Guy Marriott, senior vice president of EMI Music, said the industry welcomed the rapidly growing use of the Internet as a medium to listen to music.
But he said governments must act to prevent people from downloading music on the Internet and distributing it without compensating artists and record companies.
"If you don't stamp on a tiny irritant now, it has the potential to be a big irritant in future years," he said.
Carlos Pinto, managing director of Sony Music in Portugal, said: "If we can't control this problem from the beginning, the record industry could be in danger very soon."

Representatives of the music industry meeting in Lisbon said it was hard to estimate how many people now listened to music on the Internet, but they all agreed that it would be a major medium in the future.

A recent study by Internet consultancy Jupiter said that some $1.6 billion worth of recorded music would be sold on-line in the United States in 2002, up from $18.2 million in 1996 and an expected $47 million this year.

The record industry executives were reviewing progress by more than 100 governments towards implementing two new copyright treaties for the digital on-line era. So far none of the governments have ratified the treaties.

The treaties, signed at a World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO) conference in Geneva last December, provide the legal framework for the music industry to invest and trade in the market for on-line delivery of recordings.

Sony's Pinto said: "Unless rights holders are given the exclusive right to control their works in the digital era, the Internet will bring less security for artists and record companies, and more piracy."

He added: "Record companies will be reluctant to invest $50,000 or more on a really first class recording if they know that it can be instantly spread all over the world and copied again and again, eroding the high-risk investment that created the work."

Executives of the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), which represents record companies, said they would meet Culture Ministry officials in mid-July to press for implementation by Portugal of the copyright treaties.

IFPI Director Frances Moore said: "Our message in Lisbon is that the recording industry urgently needs investment security, and that governments should make ratification of the WIPO treaties a priority.
"The message is especially appropriate in Portugal, which has had a poor record in implementing important European Union and international copyright rules."
